---
title: "Why ordinary beta regression does not fit endpoint sliders"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The [beta distribution](../random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd) may initially look ideal for a zero-to-one slider because it can take many shapes inside that interval. But its support is the open interval $0<y<1$: exact zero and exact one are excluded.

To see why, recall the distinction between density and probability. The height of a [probability density function](../random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions.qmd) tells us how probability is concentrated around a value. Probability comes from area over an interval. An interval with identical endpoints has width zero, so

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=a)=\int_a^a f(y)\,dy=0.
$$

This remains true even if the density becomes very tall near $a$. MegaNegRaising contains recorded zeros and ones on both sliders, so the ordinary beta likelihood is undefined for some observed responses.

The [expected value](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) of the beta model describes an interior mean. The [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) holds the recorded slider values fixed while comparing shape parameters, so it cannot silently replace an endpoint with a nearby interior value.

The first empirical question is whether the problematic endpoints actually occur. Once they do, moving them inward by an amount that depends on sample size changes the recorded responses rather than repairing the ordinary beta likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: load-meganegraising-beta
#| echo: true
mnr <- read.csv("data/meganegraising/meganegraising-balanced.csv")
endpoint_counts <- data.frame(
  response = rep(c("neg-raising", "ease"), each = 3L),
  region = rep(c("zero", "interior", "one"), times = 2L),
  observations = c(sum(mnr$negraising == 0),
                   sum(mnr$negraising > 0 & mnr$negraising < 1),
                   sum(mnr$negraising == 1),
                   sum(mnr$acceptability == 0),
                   sum(mnr$acceptability > 0 & mnr$acceptability < 1),
                   sum(mnr$acceptability == 1))
)
endpoint_counts
```

For $0<y<1$, a mean–precision beta parameterization is

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\mu_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi}.
$$

Neither density value at an endpoint is a probability mass. A common workaround nudges every observation with

$$
y_i^*=\frac{y_i(n-1)+1/2}{n}.
$$

Because the consequence depends on the observed sample size, we compute it from the retained judgments below.

```{r}
#| label: actual-endpoint-nudge
#| echo: true
n <- nrow(mnr)
transform_endpoint <- function(y) (y * (n - 1) + .5) / n
data.frame(recorded = c(0, 1), transformed = transform_endpoint(c(0, 1)),
           sample_size = n)
```

The dependence on sample size is visible without inventing another dataset. We apply the rule separately to the observed active-voice and passive-voice subsets, which contain different numbers of retained judgments:

```{r}
#| label: endpoint-nudge-by-sample-size
#| echo: true
n_values <- table(mnr$voice)
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(n_values), function(voice_value) {
  nn <- unname(n_values[[voice_value]])
  data.frame(voice = voice_value, sample_size = nn, recorded = c(0, 1),
             transformed = (c(0, 1) * (nn - 1) + .5) / nn)
}))
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-endpoint-nudge
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
plot_data <- transform(endpoint_counts,
                       probability = observations / ave(observations, response, FUN = sum))
ggplot(plot_data, aes(region, probability, shape = response, group = response)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .25), size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Observed region", y = "Proportion", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

For the `r n` retained judgments, zero becomes `r format(transform_endpoint(0), digits = 6)` and one becomes `r format(transform_endpoint(1), digits = 6)`. The transformation makes the sample size part of the measurement model: adding unrelated rows moves the transformed endpoints. It also replaces observed endpoint events with extremely interior values.

An endpoint can arise because a continuous intention was rounded to the displayed boundary or because a respondent deliberately selected the endpoint as a qualitatively meaningful response. Those mechanisms imply different measurement models. The prepared table cannot distinguish them, so an explicit endpoint-mass model states the retained assumption instead of silently moving the values.

A likelihood that contains explicit endpoint probabilities preserves the recorded response. [Ordered beta regression](ordered-beta-regression.qmd) does this for both sliders without changing or filtering either outcome.

## Recap and check

1. Does a large beta density near zero assign positive probability to the exact value zero? No. Density over a nonzero interval can be positive; mass at one exact point remains zero.
2. Why is the nudge not innocuous? It changes endpoint values when unrelated rows are added and assumes endpoints are merely interior measurements in disguise.

[Ordered beta regression](ordered-beta-regression.qmd) also makes a stronger assumption: one shared location orders zero, the interior, and one, while two cutpoints determine the endpoint masses.
